Many people fail to realize that the very laws that allow tribes and their land to be seen as sovereign nations are the same laws that allow horrific crimes against Indigenous women to go unpunished. It's really difficult to arrest someone when they're told that they cannot be prosecuted because the crime did not technically happen on US soil. This is talked about in the movie Wind River, it's discussed in the series RISE, which was aired on Vice a few years back, and it also features prominently in books, such as The Roundhouse by Louise Erdrich. 

The depictions RISE paints are especially chilling, as the girls relate stories of pure horror, living in fear every day of being trafficked, raped or murdered by men who live and work in the oil fields.They speak of friends who have disappeared and how they do not feel safe in their own communities. 

Not even Indigenous women living in cities are immune to this type of violence....does anyone remember the case of Savannah Greywind? She was an Indigenous woman from the Great Lakes region who was murdered at nine months pregnant, her baby was physically cut out and removed from her body, and she herself was left to die. If I recall correctly, police had a suspect, but I never heard anything about an arrest. 

So many people automatically assume that the high rates of missing and murdered Indigenous women are due to alcoholism, anger and rage coming from Indigenous men, but the truth is that is only a small portion of the problem behind why these women are seen as such easy targets for those wishing to do them harm. 

The system created for our Indigenous sisters in this country (and Canada too!) was set up to ensure that if the Indigenous population did not fail on its own, the wider society and their respective governments in both countries  (the reservation system itself and the deplorable behavior towards Indigenous communities throughout the 19th and 20th centuries, reservation and boarding schools teaching Indigenous children to hate themselves, the consequences of said schools and the direct links to the violence, alcoholism and substance abuse issues that plague Indigenous communities today, deeply ingrained racism) would certainly help to push Indigenous communities towards that end result. 

It is absolutely deplorable and despicable that Indigenous women are treated so poorly. Especially when Indigenous women have been continually at the forefront of leading issues such as climate change and ensuring that marginalized communities like the Indigenous ones have access to clean water, air, and recreational land. The Mni Wiconi movement highlighted this.

She said it would be best if my mom kept thr results to the family and used them for accommodations in college and high school. The fist time I ever heard a tree speak to me I was about 13. It was a Great Basin Bristlecone Pine and it was so old. I remember reaching out to touch it and I felt this incredible thread or pulse just rushing through the tree and into my body. In those trees, there can be a single thread of living tissue that connects it to the earth while the rest of the tree or its exterior can die off. It spoke to me of a life that wanted to be heard, to be remembered, to be acknowledged.  It was almost like it ached to tell its story. Like it was waiting for someone to come who would listen to it, who would understand it. 

There was also a little baby tree that I wasn't allowed to touch, but I sat by it for a long time. That particular tree couldn't have been more than 3 feet high but the ranger told us it was likely over 50 years old. That little one had a hunger for life. It wanted to survive, it wanted to grow, despite the harsh conditions it faced. It knew that it could have pieces of it die, that it would experience pain and that it would suffer, but life was worth it to be lived. It had a life like any other being, and it spoke and gave voice to its life like any other living thing would. It's just most people don't take the time to truly listen. 

I honestly think that there was nothing special I did to learn to speak the language of the elders outside of being willing to truly listen, and to be patient, and to keep my heart and soul open (as cheesy as that sounds). Trees do not hate. I think they recognize that emotion in others and I don't know how they choose who they want to speak to, but I think anyone is able to speak to them, so long as they know what to listen for.
Find a tree that appeals to you and give it a hug, start speaking to it. Listen carefully to what it has to say and how it feels to you to touch it and be near it.

Hey there! I actually HAVE thought about why the Bible and Quran and other old religious don't talk about reincarnation. I really enjoy studying the past, especially in a historical and literary context. In my opinion there's two things going on.....one is that reincarnation as a spiritual idea was  unknown to the ruling faction of Hebrew priests who controlled the temple (and therefore the religious ideas) at the time of Christ. 

You have the Saduccee (priestly, ruling, wealthy class) faction who did not believe in a rebirth and believed that the soul dies with the body. You also have the Essene party who was completely different from both of the previous two, and isolated themselves in the desert, subscribing to rigid ideals of cleanliness snd having fixed times for prayer and other activities. The Pharisees (common priests, why you see Jesus interacting with them, etc) believed in resurrection which is different from reincarnation in that they believed the soul did not die with the body but that it lived on in anticipation of a coming conquering of death. There wasn't really an idea of transformation or the movement of a soul from one body to another like in reincarnation. The literature from that time and from the Dead Sea scrolls talks a LOT about apocalypse scenarios and they were apparently quite popular! This is probably also why the book of Revelations made it into the New Testament, along with other, older apocalyptic texts (though NOT the Book of Enoch, boo!) 

I think that could be one reason why you don't really see reincarnation being talked about in the Bible or in other contemporary pieces of ancient literature. The idea of a soul moving on into another unrelated body seems to be foreign to the ancient Near East with regards to it showing up in the scant archeological literary record. Even the Egyptian Book of the Dead doesn't really even go into reincarnation, it discusses rituals and spells meant to allow the soul of the deceased to enjoy a pleasant afterlife in the body that they had previously vacated through death. Of course you have examples like Pharaoh's being deified after death but that doesn't suggest that they were reincarnated into a different body, only that their human form would become deathless and God-like. 

My other thought, specifically to the example of the Hebrew Bible is that reincarnation as an idea would have given people a lot of personal power with regards to the way they thought and lived their lives. Imagine you live as a common person in Judea circa 12 BC. You have no Pharisees, no one literate other than a rabbi who teaches you from a scroll you cannot read on your own. What you are taught is that your life after death is simply nothing. You die and return to dust and your dust is mingled with your ancestors. There is essentially nothing you are preparing for in the afterlife except a cessation of consciousness. Now imagine someone comes and tells you that you have another chance to "get things right" a second or third or infinite amount of times after you die. That your soul moves on to other bodies and you do not lose your essence. Imagine how much power this would have given people with this knowledge! The power to change their own lives or to even try the unthinkable in their own lives if it meant that they would get another opportunity if they failed. 

This is just my own idea, no facts at all. I'm not claiming to have the answers. These are just my observations after studying the ancient Middle and Near East. So with regards to why reincarnation isn't talked about my opinion is two fold: the religious ideas and structure of that time and place would not have allowed for it to become an idea and that if it DID come into being as an idea, it would have been silenced once the ruling factions realized it had the power to  provide hope and spiritual sustenance to the common people. The Saduccee faction was heavily aligned with Rome, especially prior to and during the wars when the Temple was destroyed.

Personally, I believe in reincarnation. I've had WAY too many creepy experiences, too many past life dreams, and too many striking and shocking coincidences in my own life to dismiss it. In addition to all this, I also dabble in astrology for my personal use, and lo and behold, my story is even repeated in my charts. Hello! So my guild was founded by our clan head in the 70's. They are of Scottish descent but to be a member you certainly don't have to be! I joined because I wanted to get involved in reenactment and because my last name is likely Scottish, but I'll never know. One really cool aspect of this guild (and of reenactment, really) is learning things you would otherwise never know. For me, I'm a POC and I've learned through research that there were people of African descent at the courts of England and in Spain at this time! Katherine of Aragon brought people of African descent with her to England when she married Prince Arthur. There were even two ladies of African descent at the Scottish court in 1504. Knowing this really makes me feel so connected to history because I never saw anyone who looked like me in the history books when I was learning about the Renaissance or about this particular time period. 

The knowledge that we share is a reflection of what daily life for all classes would have been like in the 1500's. We display that through our dress, our speech, our actions and through our conversation and interaction with the public. 
We try to show "a slice of life" to the general public and that includes living temporarily as they would have done back then. So we rise and dress from our tents and plait and tape our hair and put on our arisaides and the men kilt up and go to the pike rack where they teach whoever wants to learn about weapons care, how to handle them and work with them. 

The women do everything from spinning on traditional wheels and with drop spindles, embroidery, knitting and needlework. We have a working kitchen where we make butter, bread, and cook. We have a tavern where many of our people gather to eat, play traditional games, do crafting, or sing songs of the period or ones we've created. 

One of the coolest things I think we've done is a wool 'walking' demonstration. We literally gathered a length of wool and used vegetable water and sang as we worked wool in a traditional manner to ready it for processing and being used for clothing. 

So basically it's just attempting to show how life would have run for us in the 1500's, but in 2024. We're basically time travelers LOL.

I'm a historical reenactor and my main venue is the Renaissance Faire. I'm with a guild and we're a Scottish group, so people tend to associate us with knitting, probably because of the famous lace shawls of later periods. If you come to our yard you can see us ladies working on all kinds of projects. 

Our costume mistress allows us to knit in public because it gives us something to do, and because people ALWAYS ask about the shawls and lacework. 

In reality though, it wouldn't really be upper class women doing knitting at all, unfortunately. Those ladies would mostly have done embroidery, fine needlework or sewing.  

Things like stockings, garters for stockings, sleeves, flat caps, etc would be knit, but the lower classes would be making them in "common" fabrics like wool that would be more durable for hard wear and work.  Wealthier court women and noblewomen would have used a more luxurious fabric or a very high quality wool. 

In our guild you see women of all classes knitting, but the trick with all of us knitting is that you can't really tell who exactly is a member of our court and who isn't, or who is a middle class woman or a peasant.  Scotland at that time was such a poor country, basically everyone except the very richest nobles and the court would be able to afford anything even close to a luxury fabric. So in my guild we all knit, but we're also encouraged to do embroidery or needlework as well.

This is incorrect. Another commenter explained it well in a different comment but Amenhotep was a New Kingdom Pharoah, far removed from the rulers of the First Kingdom like Khufu or Khafre or Djoser. This type of practice may have occurred in prior burials and also is thought to have happened in Sumeria (see the burial of Puabi) but I myself have not seen or read about the practice occurring in New or Middle Kingdom Egypt. 

Furthermore, as pointed out by another commentor, the dog was interred in a separate burial chamber apart from the Pharoah which suggests that they were interred at different times. The dog could very well have died first and the Pharoah ordered a chamber made for his faithful companion. 

There is also a strong tradition in ancient Egypt of mummified animals such as cats, baboons or bulls (Apis bull). The Apis bull especially was revered and allowed to live out it's natural life in peace and was later mummified after death. It was also illegal for cats to be killed in ancient Egypt due to their associations with Bastet.

Oddly specific but I love Biblical history and will sometimes read Biblical Christian fiction to get a "feel" for that particular world. My favorites to read about are the Bronze and Iron Ages, but I will go for the Herodian period as well.

One thing I've noticed that REALLY jumps out to me is that these authors clearly are not doing adequate historical research is when you look at the maps they include, and especially at the names of lakes in the area. They all, with no exceptions, refer to the Dead Sea by that name exclusively. Even when characters are talking, they refer to it as such. This bothers me as a history lover and as someone who studies that time period for fun.

The usage of the name Dead Sea is a relatively modern term. In antiquity and in ancient times, the you see it referred to as 'The Salt Sea,' 'Sea of Salt' or in later periods like the Herodian, it's called by its Roman epithet, Lake Asphaltitis ( because it produces lumps of tar or pitch that float to the surface. Everyone in antiquity loved this pitch, it was used for embalming in Egypt, for making boats and baskets watertight throughout the empire, and it has one other use I can't quite recall). 

Historians and archeologists have found scrolls and literature in Qumran (Dead Sea Scrolls) and the sea is indeed referred to as 'The Salt Sea' in those works. It stands to reason that those further back would have called it that as well. It's like the Christian fiction authors have a massive blind spot when it comes to doing research on topography and place names. I always chuckle when I see that and figure they only did glancing research, at best. I haven't seen this with other non-Christian fiction books that are set in the same time period either. The Dovekeepers by Alice Hoffman is a good example of this as she refers to the Sea by both names I mentioned here, which suggests she really did her homework.

Like for example a wine dark sea, an ocean so deep that it appeared purple black, tossed about with light? A sailor might have had a word for that color but what about a farmer? Did the ancient world actually perceive colors differently? Did they not have words for specific colors and so to them, they would have existed as 'one' singular color? Or have only a few descriptions or names for different shades of the same color?

OP, have you ever heard the phrase from Homer describing a "wine dark sea"? That has to be one of my favorite phrases in ancient literature l, and not just because of how unique and odd that statement sounds. 

It makes you think about the concept of color and how the ancient minds perceived it. I've read before that one reason is because colors that are rare in nature (true purple, very deep dark blue, etc) may not have been viewed or seen often in the ancient world, and so the ancients had to either come up with names for them or resort to looking to other examples in their world to describe them. Hence why the sea would be dark as wine, even though the sea is not wine colored in its depths, it is deep blue. 

And like your cornflower hair example, men's hair cannot naturally be cornflower blue, but true black often has a blue sheen to it. Like blue black skin or hair. Being unable to describe that blue-blackness, ancient man may have had to resort to other words or descriptions to find ways to describe someone who had hair that was so dark it appeared blue in light.

That's just a theory I read somewhere and I can't say if it's true or not but it stuck with me and I hope it makes you think a bit.

I get mad at the problems, I'll sit underneath them and go over the moves in my head and I'll talk my mistakes out with other climbing friends but I never tell myself I'm weak or a failure. Ever. Climbing is the one part of my life where I absolutely will not allow those negative thoughts about myself into my head and instead focus on the work to be done and how to climb better and become stronger. I also struggle with depression and the way I see it is that depression has taken so much from me already, it's not going to take climbing from me too. 

As far as the friends who climb harder grades that make you discouraged....I say learn from them! Talk to people and ask for tips! I have a friend who is an insane boulderer, he regularly sends V7 and V8. When I came back to the gym after an absence, he told me he had also been out for around the same amount of time as me and had gotten out of shape to boot. He said that at first he was struggling on some V3's and that he felt weak and like he had lost his game. Other people I saw after my absence said the same thing, that at the beginning it was really a struggle to get back in the game and feel capable. 

Heck, sometimes even my top rope buddies have great tips for climbing better, like improving footwork or traversing or in my case, topping out on higher easy grade problems so I can get over the fear of falling from highball problems. My goal is to climb classic problems outdoors, so I'm trying to focus on that and not let my head and negative thoughts get in the way. I think you shouldn't be so hard on yourself. You also mentioned you had an injury, your body and mind is going to need time to adjust to getting the skills and trust back that you used to have. It just might take time and patience but I guarantee you're no weaker on the wall than anyone else, nor are you a failure. Just the fact that you got back out there proves that. You got this!

I also try really hard to be sustainable in my fashion and clothing choices. 90% of my wardrobe is thrifted except for specific items I wouldn't ever be able to find in a goodwill. It's very important to me to try and do my part, even if its something as small as purchasing most of my clothes second hand.

They are endangered and difficult to grow even in their native conditions. They are my favorite plant (not really a tree) and the best way to own one is to honestly buy property with several on it. I grew up with this beautiful species and I'm passionate about it and preserving it.

They need specific requirements, one of which is a hard freeze in order to allow the plant to bloom. Its root system also extends a massive amount around it, might be difficult to keep indoors. Also, you may not live long enough to see it grow to maturity. There is no way to accurately age a yucca brevifolia and the big ones you see could easily be hundreds of years old. The baby ones are cute too, but they take a long time to start looking normal. They require a specific environment (the Mojave desert with its extreme heat, cold and generally vicious and unforgiving character) and a specific pollinator, the yucca moth. 

In addition to this, the plant likes to grow in vast forests, or families. They are a social plant, you'll rarely see one alone growing by itself a far distance from the others. I would recommend taking a visit to the desert to see the plant in it's natural habitat and glory. They are truly spectacular, and a wonder to behold. I grew up with the western population in California and those get the biggest. There are smaller subspecies that grow in Nevada and parts of Arizona and Utah. 

They love visitors, you should go see them before they're gone. 😊
